processes.description: The desk lead, Bill Williams III, tells the traders when a counterparty is halted or cleared again, for example no trades with Sempra until further notice, or WWP being good to buy and sell with again. Notices from others are passed on too: how a counterparty that wants to terminate must send its termination letter by fax, and a forwarded notice about AEP Energy Services taking effect at a stated time that day. Each round is a one-way notice that traders read and act on.
steps: The desk lead or credit learns that a counterparty is halted, suspended, terminating or cleared again.
A short notice naming the counterparty and its status is written or forwarded to the traders.
Termination notices say how the counterparty must deliver its letter; suspension notices say when they take effect.
Traders read the notice and stop or resume dealing with that counterparty.

automation.approach: Keep one counterparty status list owned by credit that feeds deal entry, so halted counterparties are blocked when a deal is entered, and send every status change to the trading desks in a fixed notice naming the counterparty, the new status, when it takes effect and what traders must do.
automation.rationale: Rounds are short one-way notices written freehand in different styles, from a single capitalised line to forwarded legal notices. A fixed notice layout makes the status, effective time and required action unmistakable and can be used straight away, while blocking at deal entry needs system work first.

work_estimate.rationale: Beyond the notice itself, a round means confirming the counterparty's status with credit and updating the desk's counterparty list or deal entry so traders stop or resume dealing. That is about 5 minutes; as little as 2 when a notice is only relayed, up to 15 when the change must be set up in more than one place.

processes.description: A round is one dated credit report: Darron Giron forwards the report for a trading date, titled with that date, to Carole Frank in the credit group, and a few other credit staff read it too. The report carries counterparty positions and exposure from the risk books. Most rounds are bare forwards; notes appear only when reports are late, as after a systems problem or an absence, when reports for several dates go together. In a later round credit asks that Risk and Credit Aggregation pull the same post IDs so counterparty exposure reconciles.
steps: Pull the counterparty position and exposure report for the trading date from the risk books.
Save it as the credit report titled with that trading date.
Forward it to the credit group contact, who reads it with other credit staff.
When systems fail or the preparer is away, send the missed reports together later with a note.
When credit reconciles exposure, make sure risk and credit aggregation pull the same post IDs.

stalls.summary: A systems problem held up distribution of the report, and the preparer apologised for the late send.
While the preparer was out, reports were not sent; on his return reports for several trading dates went out together, with a note that he did not know whether the recipient had received any of them.
Reports also go out well after the trading date they cover, with earlier dates' reports forwarded together in one go.
Counterparty exposure could not be reconciled until Risk and Credit Aggregation pulled the same post IDs.

automation.approach: Generate the credit report from the official post each night and send it to a credit distribution list, with a check that flags any trading date with no report sent and confirms that the post ID used matches the one credit aggregation pulls.
automation.rationale: The report itself is routine and comes from the risk system; what goes wrong is coverage and consistency. Reports pile up when the one sender is away or systems fail, and credit needs the same post IDs as risk to reconcile. A written procedure lets a backup run and send the report and fixes the post ID rule; scheduled distribution then removes the manual forward.

work_estimate.rationale: A round means running or pulling the counterparty position and exposure report for the trading date, checking it ran on the right post, and saving it for sending. The quotes show a routine generated report with no rework beyond late or batched sends, so about 10 minutes; 5 when it runs cleanly, up to 30 when systems problems or post ID reconciliation get in the way.

processes.description: Risk analysts keep the forward curve files and the mapping of curves, locations and post IDs to books in the risk system. A round starts when a new curve is set up and must be added to Tagg or the publication names, when a book owner is asked how a location should be mapped, or when the nightly official post ID is run and passed on. Dated curve files and post ID lists are forwarded to other groups. The last rounds rebuild curve lists and mappings for Netco, moving modified curve files to a new directory ready to load for portcalc.
steps: A new or changed curve or location is set up and flagged for mapping.
The analyst asks the book owner how it should be mapped and waits for the answer.
The curve is added to the publication names and Tagg, and its mapping is entered in the risk system.
The official post ID macro queries the official books and the night's post ID is sent on.
Dated curve files and lists of new or changed post IDs are forwarded to the groups that use them.
For Netco, curve lists are rebuilt, retired curves' locations are listed and remapped, and modified files are loaded.

stalls.summary: Mapping changes wait on the book owner's decision about how a curve or location should be mapped.
The nightly official post ID run is not done reliably: one colleague is named as running the macro most nights, and the thread asks that it be done every night.
The work depends on individuals: files were handed over just before a colleague changed groups, and checks for another region were done only because its owner was out.

The Netco move forces rework: curve files must be modified before use in the new environment, locations mapped to curves no longer set must be listed and remapped, a full curve list is needed, and files move to a new directory ahead of a load deadline.

contradictions.summary: Instructions on where curve material lives change: one note gives the shared-drive location where the curve lists are saved, and a later note announces a new directory for the curve files.

automation.approach: Keep one master table of curves, locations, post IDs and book mappings, with a check that flags locations mapped to curves no longer set and new curves missing from Tagg or the publication names. Schedule the official post ID macro every night and send the post ID and the list of changed post IDs to the groups that use them.
automation.rationale: The work rests on a few people's knowledge, handed over as files when someone changes groups and covered as needed when someone is out. A written procedure for adding and mapping a curve and running the nightly post lets anyone cover. The master table and scheduled macro then take over the repetitive lookups, while mapping decisions stay with the book owners.

work_estimate.rationale: A round means setting up or changing curves, entering mappings in the risk system and Tagg, running the post ID macro across the official books, or building lists of curves and remapped locations for Netco. A single curve change takes about 15 minutes; a typical round with checks about 30; list-building and file changes for the Netco move up to 90.
